text: I was tired at the end.
Twelve people were in the room.
Good morning, Paula. So, how was the visit on Friday?
It was long. The drive was three hours, and the factory was huge.
Was the meeting in the plant or in an office?
In a meeting room, and it was crowded. Twelve people were there.
No, they weren't. Six were engineers, and the others were from the client's finance team.
And the technical manager? People say he is not easy.
He was difficult at the start. His questions were very difficult for me.
After lunch the room was quiet and he was patient with me. It was useful. I was tired, but it was a good day.
I am surprised. Your first visit alone, twelve people, and three hours on the road.
I was surprised too. On Friday morning I was worried. On Friday night I was not.
It was long. The room was crowded.
The questions were difficult, but it was useful.
No, they weren't. Six were engineers.

Hi, Paula. David here. Today your lesson is about two very small words, was and were, and I want to tell you why they matter more than they look. When I came back from my first site visit, my manager asked me one question. How was it? And I said, it was fine. That was all. Fine. Two days later he asked me again, and this time he said, no, tell me how it was. Was the room crowded? Were the questions difficult? Were you tired at the end? And I started to talk, and I talked for ten minutes. He was not testing my English, Paula. He was teaching me something, and it took me years to understand it. A report says what happened. But how was it says what it was like, and that is the part people remember. So when somebody asks you how the visit was, please do not say fine. Say the drive was long. Say the room was crowded. Say the manager was difficult at the start. Say you were tired, but it was useful. Five short sentences, and now your colleague was there with you. That is the whole lesson. See you soon.

Good morning, Paula. Sofia here. I read your report from the visit on Friday, and I want to say three things. First, the numbers were right. Twelve people, six hours, fourteen technical questions. Nobody in this team writes a report that clean, so thank you. Second, and this is the important one, I called the client on Monday. The technical manager said your questions were good. He said you were slow, and then he said something I really want you to hear. He said, she was slow because she was careful, and careful is exactly what we want in a large risk. Third. Do you remember, in January, when you told me you were not ready to go alone? You were wrong, and I am very happy you were wrong. On Friday morning you were worried. On Friday night you were the person who did it. Paula, in November you will be in Miami, and somebody there will ask you, how was your first visit alone? Please do not say it was fine. Tell them everything. It was long, it was crowded, it was difficult, and it was yours. See you Thursday.
It was long. The room was crowded.
The questions were difficult, but it was useful.
I wasn't tired on Friday morning.
No, they weren't. Six were engineers.
